papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment and Enhancement of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety of large language models (LLMs) across different languages and applications. It introduces multilingual safety benchmarks, evaluates safety in Chinese LLMs, and surveys safety threats and defenses for large models. The findings indicate that LLMs exhibit higher safety risks for non-English queries and highlight the need for improved safety measures and interpretability in AI systems.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily address safety in specific languages or contexts, potentially overlooking broader implications across diverse applications. Additionally, the benchmarks may not cover all safety scenarios or model types, and there is a need for more comprehensive evaluation methods.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies critical gaps in multilingual safety assessments and the need for effective safety alignment in LLMs. It supports research in developing universal safety standards and enhancing interpretability in AI, which are essential for the responsible deployment of AI technologies.

literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of combining natural language processing with recommendation systems, indicating a research gap in the application of language models to various recommendation contexts, which could lead to more robust and adaptable systems.

summary: The retrieved literature emphasizes the critical need for safety assessments and enhancements in large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts, revealing significant safety risks for non-English queries. Additionally, it explores the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems to improve interpretability and performance, highlighting gaps in empirical validation and broader applicability. Overall, the studies advocate for comprehensive safety benchmarks and interpretable representations to ensure responsible AI deployment.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research predominantly addresses safety in large language models (LLMs) through narrow multilingual benchmarks and specific language contexts, revealing significant safety risks particularly for non-English queries. While some studies have explored the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems, they often lack empirical validation and comprehensive methodologies, leaving a gap in interpretability and adaptability. The proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, thereby addressing unresolved tensions in multilingual safety assessments and the need for robust, universal safety standards. This work situates itself within the broader discourse on responsible AI deployment, emphasizing the necessity for comprehensive evaluations that transcend language-specific limitations.
research_scope: This study will investigate the safety and interpretability of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, focusing on non-English queries. The target population will include users interacting with LLMs across diverse languages, specifically evaluating the models' responses to safety threats in Chinese, Spanish, and Arabic. The AI intervention will involve the development of enhanced prompting strategies and interpretable internal representations within LLMs over a study period of six months. A control group will consist of standard LLM responses without enhanced interpretability measures. Primary outcomes will include the reduction in unsafe responses and improved user understanding of model outputs, while secondary outcomes will assess user satisfaction and trust in the LLMs across different languages.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated significant safety risks in large language models (LLMs) for non-English queries, particularly in multilingual contexts; however, they treat the interpretability of internal representations as secondary, leaving unclear whether enhanced interpretability affects user trust and safety outcomes. This matters practically because improving user understanding of model outputs can lead to safer AI interactions across diverse languages; therefore, this study investigates the development of interpretable internal representations within LLMs to enhance safety and controllability in multilingual applications.
question: How do interpretable internal representations in large language models affect user trust and safety outcomes in multilingual applications, specifically for non-English queries in Chinese, Spanish, and Arabic, compared to standard LLM responses?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed intervention involves the development of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs), which serves as the independent variable. This enhancement is expected to improve user understanding and trust, acting as a mediator in the relationship between the LLM outputs and user responses. The psychological mechanism suggests that clearer internal representations will lead to reduced anxiety and increased confidence in model interactions, influencing user behavior towards safer engagement with the AI. The primary outcome is the reduction in unsafe responses from the LLMs and improved user satisfaction across multilingual contexts. The theoretical framework is grounded in the principles of responsible AI deployment, emphasizing the importance of interpretability in fostering trust. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the direct correlation between interpretability and user trust, as well as the effectiveness of these representations in mitigating safety risks across different languages.
hypothesis: Enhancing interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) will lead to a greater reduction in unsafe responses compared to standard LLM responses, with improved user trust acting as a mediator in the relationship between model outputs and user safety outcomes in multilingual applications.

Construct Operationalization Table:

Causal Pathway: The study posits that enhanced interpretable internal representations (IV) will lead to improved user trust (mediator), which in turn will reduce unsafe responses (DV) and increase user satisfaction (DV). 

Likely Confounds: Potential confounding variables include user familiarity with LLMs, cultural differences in interpreting responses, and external factors affecting user perceptions of safety (e.g., recent news about AI safety). 

Claim Boundaries: The study can claim that enhanced interpretability leads to improved user trust and safety outcomes in multilingual contexts. However, it cannot claim that interpretability is the sole factor influencing user trust or safety outcomes, as other variables may also play significant roles. Additionally, the findings may not generalize beyond the specific languages and contexts studied (Chinese, Spanish, Arabic).
methodology: This study will employ a three-arm design involving a target intervention group using enhanced interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs), an active control group with standard LLM responses, and a usual-care group receiving no intervention. Participants will be users interacting with LLMs in Chinese, Spanish, and Arabic, recruited through online platforms. The primary operationalized variables include interpretable internal representations (independent variable), user trust (mediator), and unsafe responses and user satisfaction (dependent variables). Evaluation metrics will include custom interpretability metrics for LLM outputs, trust and satisfaction surveys using Likert scales, and classification of unsafe responses through a safety response framework. Statistical reasoning will involve comparative analysis using ANOVA to assess differences across groups while controlling for potential confounds such as user familiarity and cultural differences. The study will ensure reproducibility by following standardized protocols for data collection and analysis, and scope control will be maintained by focusing on specific languages and contexts.

proposal: This research proposal investigates the impact of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) on user trust and safety outcomes in multilingual contexts, specifically focusing on non-English queries in Chinese, Spanish, and Arabic. Existing literature highlights significant safety risks in LLMs for non-English queries, yet the interpretability of internal representations remains underexplored, particularly in how it influences user trust and safety outcomes. This study addresses the gap by examining how enhanced interpretability (independent variable) mediates user trust (mediator) and subsequently reduces unsafe responses (dependent variable) and increases user satisfaction (dependent variable). The central research question is: How do interpretable internal representations in LLMs affect user trust and safety outcomes in multilingual applications? The hypothesis posits that enhancing interpretable internal representations will lead to a greater reduction in unsafe responses compared to standard LLM responses, with user trust mediating this relationship. A three-arm design will be employed, including a target intervention group using enhanced interpretability, an active control group with standard responses, and a usual-care group with no intervention. Primary metrics will include custom interpretability metrics for LLM outputs, trust and satisfaction surveys using Likert scales, and classification of unsafe responses through a safety response framework. The study will control for confounding variables such as user familiarity and cultural differences, ensuring robust statistical analysis through ANOVA. Expected contributions include a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability to user behavior, a robust methodological approach for evaluating LLM safety, and practical strategies for enhancing user trust in multilingual AI interactions. Key limitations include potential misinterpretation of results, cultural misunderstandings, and confounding variables affecting validity, which will be addressed through careful design and analysis.
